vignette: Ten years ago, during a tour across the Pacific, Elias found himself in a cramped hostel room in Auckland. He trusted the man he’d been drinking with for years. The shift happened slowly, then all at once. There was no fight that made sense, just the heavy weight of a body pressing him into the mattress, the smell of cheap whiskey and stale smoke, the desperate, silent bargaining that happens when the nervous system short-circuits. When it was over, Elias stood in the shower until the water ran cold, scrubbing skin raw, convinced he could wash the violation out of him. He left the next morning without telling anyone. Now at forty-five, Elias runs the pass at a coastal bistro in Rarotonga. The kitchen breathes around him: steam rising from the rice cooker, the sharp crack of knives against timber, the rhythmic call of the service bell. He used to love the order of it. Control. But lately, the pass feels like a cage. When the dinner rush hits, the air grows thick and close. He watches the line cook behind him, hyperaware of every shift in proximity. A stray hand brushing his shoulder to pass a pan sends his breath hitching. He flinches, then covers it by loudly calling the next ticket order. His kitchen has become a map of safe distances and controlled movements. He never lets anyone stand behind him. He wears long sleeves in the heat, though the other cooks joke about his stubbornness. The chef’s coat, once a uniform of pride, now feels like armor. Sleep has become a foreign country. When he finally drifts off, the dreams return with the same suffocating clarity. He wakes sweating, heart hammering against his ribs, staring at the ceiling while the island wind rattles the blinds. During the day, the world feels perpetually tilted. Grocery shopping triggers a low, constant hum of dread. He avoids the checkout lanes when possible, preferring to pay at the back door. At the market, the press of bodies near his hips makes him step back, pretending to examine the taro roots. He drinks less now, though he misses the old numbness. Instead, he channels everything into the plate. He plates each dish with surgical precision, arranging each leaf and drizzle exactly as he visualizes it, as if perfect symmetry could keep the chaos at bay. When a server drops a tray during a slow Tuesday, his hands jerk toward his own arms before he forces them to stay at his sides. His divorce two years ago felt less like a sudden break and more like a slow retreat. He tells people it was because of the restaurant’s demands, but the truth is quieter. Intimacy now reads as a threat. He stops conversations before they go too deep, deflects with humor, and has learned to leave dinners early. His whānua checks in on him, but he answers with short messages and polite deflections. The silence between him and his heritage has grown heavy. He used to cook family feasts for hundreds, the kind that filled courtyards with laughter and smoke. Now he cooks alone, tasting only salt and steel. Tonight, the service wind-down settles. Elias wipes down the pass, the stainless steel reflecting a face older than forty-five. The head waiter asks if he wants to go for drinks after. Elias shakes his head, saying he’s tired. He walks to his car alone, feeling the familiar check of his body—doors locked, keys ready, route mapped. He sits in the driver’s seat for a long moment, listening to the engine tick as it cools, breathing in the quiet dark before stepping back into the long work of staying here.
